prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a single, well-defined invention: Katori's magic-wavelength trapping removes Doppler, recoil and Stark shifts while many atoms are interrogated in parallel, and Ye's group drove it to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 with many-body-enhanced operation. It is independently reproduced in strontium, ytterbium and mercury at several national laboratories, international comparisons are routine, and it underpins the planned redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy and laboratory tests of varying constants. Four members place it in their top three or first place, which I treat only as a signal to test, but the underlying case is that it has a concrete before-and-after, a clean two-person attribution and no real maturity question.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty and timing. The 2005 prize (frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (single-quantum-system control, including ion clocks) honoured neighbouring precursors, and Ye's comb and ultrastable-laser work sits close to the 2005 recognition. The redefinition of the second is still pending, so the committee could argue that the decisive societal payoff has not yet arrived, and that other groups (NIST, PTB, SYRTE) share credit in ways a two-name prize does not reflect.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks trapped-ion quantum logic (Cirac, Zoller, Blatt) first as a thirty-year, widely confirmed platform that turned quantum information processing into a laboratory discipline.
responses.response: I accept the influence of the Cirac-Zoller proposal, but I disagree on attribution and overlap. Wineland's 2012 prize already covered the experimental control of trapped ions, and the first entangling gates came substantially from NIST and Innsbruck groups, so the experimental share credited to Blatt is contestable, as Mehlig acknowledges. The lattice clock has a cleaner invention-to-demonstration chain and a smaller overlap with earlier prizes, so I keep B008 ahead of B022.

responses.point: Olsson places aberration-corrected electron microscopy first as a clear invention that overcame the Scherzer limit and made atomic-resolution imaging routine across materials science.
responses.response: I agree the achievement is real, mature and overdue, and I rank it fourth, so it is my first alternative. Where I differ is on breadth of fundamental physics. The clock opens measurement of relativistic time dilation, constants and a new SI second, whereas the corrector is primarily an enabling tool whose payoff is realised in materials and chemistry. I also share her concern that Krivanek's STEM corrector work complicates the three-name credit, and that the field boundary with chemistry is a risk.

responses.point: Danielsson puts the ATLAS and CMS Higgs discovery first, arguing the 2013 prize covered theory and the experimental discovery is overdue, with spokespersons and founders as the defensible names.
responses.response: The scientific significance is beyond doubt and I do not dispute it. My serious reservation is attribution: thousands of authors in two collaborations, and a three-person limit forces an arbitrary choice among Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee, which Olsson also flags with a different three. As an experimentalist from large collaborations I would not want a prize to rest on a spokesperson convention, which is why I put the discovery below a prize with a clean credited set. I would revisit this if the committee finds a principled rule for the names.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as core atomic physics, with Katori and Ye as the natural pair and many independent groups reproducing and surpassing the original performance.
responses.response: I agree and note it matches my own reading. I would add his point about Sr, Yb and Hg reproduction to the maturity case, and I share his caution that the wider ecosystem of comb and ultrastable-laser technology is outside this credit. Where I would qualify his view is on timing: with the SI redefinition pending, I do not think that is a reason to wait, but we should say in the citation that the prize is for the invention and development of the clock itself.

uncertainties: Whether Ye's frequency-comb and ultrastable-laser contributions overlap with the 2005 prize enough to reduce the standing of the clock itself.
Whether other strontium and ytterbium clock pioneers deserve credit that a two-name prize omits; I rely on recalled history rather than verified sources.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the SI redefinition of the second before awarding.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B008 from the provided profile. My documented connections (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur, KTH) concern astroparticle detectors; B042 (IceCube) is in my general field of cosmic-ray and astroparticle science, and I list it only as an alternative, but I flag the field proximity in case the committee wishes to consider recusal there.
